splits.legalQuestion: Whether the rule of lenity takes priority over agency deference (Auer/Kisor deference) when interpreting ambiguous provisions in the Sentencing Guidelines that affect criminal liability or sentencing enhancements.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether courts should defer to the Sentencing Commission's anti-defendant interpretations of ambiguous Guidelines provisions or instead apply the rule of lenity in favor of the defendant. This matters because it determines whether agencies can effectively expand criminal punishment through regulatory interpretation rather than through the legislative process.

positions.label: Lenity trumps deference
positions.summary: Holds that the rule of lenity takes precedence over agency deference when interpreting ambiguous criminal sentencing provisions, preventing agencies from using delegated authority to expand criminal liability.

positions.label: Deference trumps lenity
positions.summary: Holds that agency deference to the Sentencing Commission's commentary controls over the rule of lenity when interpreting ambiguous Guidelines provisions, even in criminal sentencing contexts.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Sentencing Guidelines' Application Note 1 to U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2, which adds inchoate offenses (conspiracy, attempt, aiding and abetting) to the definition of 'controlled substance offense,' is a valid and authoritative interpretation of the guideline after Kisor v. Wilkie.
splits.description: Circuits are divided on whether the Sentencing Commission's commentary expanding the career-offender guideline's definition of 'controlled substance offense' to include inchoate offenses is entitled to deference, given that the guideline text itself does not mention such offenses. This split affects whether defendants with prior conspiracy or attempt convictions qualify for significantly enhanced sentences under the career-offender provision.

positions.label: Commentary is valid and controlling
positions.summary: Holds that Application Note 1's inclusion of inchoate offenses is a permissible interpretation of an ambiguous guideline and is entitled to controlling deference under Stinson and Kisor.

positions.label: Commentary exceeds guideline text
positions.summary: Holds that the guideline text unambiguously excludes inchoate offenses, so Application Note 1 impermissibly expands the definition beyond what the text supports and is not entitled to deference.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the word 'and' in the First Step Act's safety-valve provision, 18 U.S.C. § 3553(f)(1), is conjunctive (requiring all three criminal-history criteria to disqualify a defendant) or disjunctive (requiring only one criterion to disqualify).
splits.description: Circuits are deeply split on whether defendants are disqualified from safety-valve relief only if they meet all three criminal-history criteria listed in § 3553(f)(1), or whether possessing any one criterion is disqualifying. This directly affects whether district courts must impose mandatory minimum sentences on drug offenders with varying criminal histories.

positions.label: 'And' is conjunctive (all three required)
positions.summary: Holds that defendants are disqualified from safety-valve relief only if they satisfy all three criminal-history criteria, reading 'and' in its ordinary conjunctive sense.

positions.label: 'And' is disjunctive (any one suffices)
positions.summary: Holds that possessing any one of the three criminal-history criteria is sufficient to disqualify a defendant from safety-valve relief, reading 'and' as disjunctive or distributive in context.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' under the Sentencing Guidelines (U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2(b)) when the state criminalizes a substance not listed on the federal controlled substances schedules.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether the Guidelines' definition of 'controlled substance offense' requires that the substance at issue be federally scheduled, or whether any state-law drug offense qualifies regardless of federal scheduling. This affects the career-offender enhancement and other Guidelines provisions tied to prior drug convictions.

positions.label: State scheduling controls (no federal match required)
positions.summary: Holds that the Guidelines broadly define 'controlled substance offense' to include any offense under state law, without requiring the substance to be federally controlled.

positions.label: Federal scheduling required
positions.summary: Holds that a state drug offense qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' only if the substance at issue is also controlled under the federal Controlled Substances Act.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a non-retroactive change in sentencing law (such as the First Step Act's amendments to 18 U.S.C. § 924(c) stacking provisions) can constitute or contribute to 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether courts may consider non-retroactive changes in sentencing law as a basis for compassionate release. Some circuits hold that such changes can never contribute to extraordinary and compelling reasons, while others permit courts to consider them, particularly after the Sentencing Commission's 2024 amendment to U.S.S.G. § 1B1.13(b)(6). This affects thousands of prisoners serving sentences under since-repealed mandatory minimums.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes cannot support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that a non-retroactive change in sentencing law cannot contribute to a finding of extraordinary and compelling reasons for sentence reduction under § 3582(c)(1)(A), and that the Sentencing Commission's policy statement permitting it exceeds the Commission's statutory authority.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes may support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that non-retroactive changes in sentencing law, particularly when combined with other factors, may be considered as part of the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis, consistent with the Sentencing Commission's amended policy statement.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a federal prisoner challenging a BOP decision regarding conditions of confinement (such as denial of First Step Act earned time credits or transfer to prerelease custody) must proceed via habeas corpus or may use a civil rights action (e.g., Bivens).
splits.description: A longstanding circuit split exists on whether habeas corpus is the exclusive remedy for federal prisoners challenging conditions of confinement that affect the duration or manner of custody, or whether civil rights actions are also available. This affects prisoners challenging BOP decisions on earned time credits, halfway house placement, and other conditions under the First Step Act.

positions.label: Habeas is not the exclusive remedy for conditions claims
positions.summary: Holds that prisoners may bring civil rights or other statutory claims to challenge conditions of confinement that do not directly challenge the fact or duration of imprisonment, even when those conditions affect custody terms.

positions.label: Habeas is exclusive for challenges to fact/duration of confinement
positions.summary: Holds that when a prisoner's claim effectively challenges the fact or duration of confinement, habeas corpus is the exclusive federal remedy and civil rights actions are unavailable.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether post-petition, pre-conversion increases in the equity of a debtor's asset belong to the bankruptcy estate or to the debtor upon good-faith conversion from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7 under 11 U.S.C. § 348(f)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether appreciation in property value between the filing of a Chapter 13 petition and conversion to Chapter 7 inures to the bankruptcy estate or remains with the debtor. This split affects debtors who experience significant property appreciation during their Chapter 13 case before converting to Chapter 7 liquidation.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the estate
positions.summary: Holds that the plain language of § 348(f)(1)(A), read together with § 541(a)'s broad definition of estate property, means that post-petition appreciation in property value belongs to the bankruptcy estate upon conversion.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the debtor
positions.summary: Holds that the Bankruptcy Code's structure and legislative history establish that post-petition, pre-conversion appreciation belongs to the debtor, not the estate, upon good-faith conversion from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the appeal deadline for a Hyde Amendment attorney's fees order in a criminal case is governed by the civil appeal deadline (30 days under Fed. R. App. P. 4(a)) or the criminal appeal deadline (14 days under Fed. R. App. P. 4(b)).
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees, though arising from a criminal case, is a civil matter subject to the longer 30-day appeal deadline or a criminal matter subject to the shorter 14-day deadline. This affects whether defendants' appeals of fee denials are timely filed.

positions.label: Civil deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment fee motion is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case, so the 30-day civil appeal deadline under Rule 4(a) governs.

positions.label: Criminal deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment fee motion is part of the criminal case, so the 14-day criminal appeal deadline under Rule 4(b) governs.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether district courts may expressly impose a revocation sentence for supervised release as punishment for the violation of supervised release conditions, or whether revocation sentences must be oriented solely toward reentry and rehabilitation.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the permissible purposes of revocation sentences for supervised release violations. Some circuits allow district courts to punish the breach of trust inherent in supervised release violations, while others hold that such sentences should focus on the defendant's successful reentry. This affects sentencing at hundreds of revocation hearings annually.

positions.label: Punishment for violation is permissible
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may expressly punish defendants for their violations of supervised release conditions at revocation proceedings.

positions.label: Revocation sentences should focus on reentry
positions.summary: Holds that revocation sentences should be oriented toward the defendant's successful reentry into society, not punishment for the supervised release violation itself.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a multiemployer pension plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability after the statutory measurement date (the end of the prior plan year), or whether all such assumptions must be fixed by that date.
splits.description: Circuits disagreed on the timing requirements for actuarial assumptions used in calculating employer withdrawal liability under ERISA. This affects billions of dollars in potential obligations because the timing of when assumptions are selected directly controls how much withdrawing employers must pay multiemployer pension plans.

positions.label: Assumptions must be fixed by measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that actuarial assumptions must be selected and fixed by the statutory measurement date (end of the prior plan year), providing employers with greater predictability about potential liability.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of IAM National Pension Fund

positions.label: Assumptions may be selected after measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that the actuary may select or update actuarial assumptions after the statutory measurement date, allowing the use of more current information in calculating withdrawal liability.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: UFCW Local 1500 Pension Fund v. Mayer Bros.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the term of supervised release is tolled (paused) when a supervisee absconds from supervision, thereby extending the period during which the person can be found to have violated the conditions of supervised release.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether federal courts may apply a judicially-created 'fugitive tolling' doctrine to supervised release, effectively extending the period of court-ordered conditions beyond the time specified in the judgment when a person absconds. This affects sentencing calculations at revocation hearings for thousands of individuals who abscond from supervised release each year.

positions.label: Tolling applies
positions.summary: Holds that the supervised release term is tolled while a supervisee is a fugitive, extending the court's authority to revoke supervised release beyond the originally specified term.

positions.label: Tolling does not apply
positions.summary: Holds that there is no statutory basis for tolling supervised release when a supervisee absconds, and the term expires as originally set regardless of the supervisee's fugitive status.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2244(b)(1)'s bar on relitigating previously raised claims in habeas proceedings applies to federal prisoners filing motions under 28 U.S.C. § 2255.
splits.description: Circuits are split 6-to-3 on whether federal prisoners face the categorical bar of § 2244(b)(1) — which prohibits raising any previously presented claim — when filing successive § 2255 motions, in addition to § 2255(h)'s separate gatekeeping requirements. This determines whether federal prisoners are subject to a stricter standard than Congress may have intended for successive collateral attacks.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) applies to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that § 2244(b)(1)'s bar on previously raised claims applies to federal prisoners filing successive § 2255 motions, categorically barring relitigation of any previously presented claim.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) does not apply to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that § 2244(b)(1) does not apply to successive § 2255 motions filed by federal prisoners, who need only satisfy § 2255(h)'s requirements of newly discovered evidence or a new rule of constitutional law.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a candidate for federal office has Article III standing to challenge a state law that allows the counting of mail-in ballots received after Election Day.
splits.description: Circuits have disagreed on the standards for evaluating whether candidates have standing to bring pre-election challenges to voting procedures. The resolution affects the ability to challenge mail-in voting rules, ballot counting deadlines, and other election administration practices before elections take place, and determines whether such disputes must wait until post-election litigation.

positions.label: Candidates have standing for pre-election challenges
positions.summary: Holds that candidates suffer a cognizable competitive injury from state election laws that allegedly dilute lawful votes or change the rules of the election, granting them Article III standing to challenge such laws before an election.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

positions.label: Candidates lack standing absent concrete injury
positions.summary: Holds that a candidate's generalized competitive interest is insufficient for Article III standing and that the candidate must demonstrate a concrete, particularized injury traceable to the challenged law.

circuits.name: Third Circuit
circuits.caseName: Donald J. Trump for President, Inc. v. Secretary of Pennsylvania

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the denial of a motion to seal documents containing private medical information is immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine.
splits.description: Circuits have taken different approaches to whether orders denying motions to seal sensitive medical records qualify for immediate appellate review under the collateral order doctrine. The D.C. Circuit held that such orders are immediately appealable because medical privacy is a value of 'high order,' while other circuits have been more restrictive in applying the collateral order doctrine to sealing disputes.

positions.label: Immediately appealable
positions.summary: Holds that denial of a motion to seal medical records is immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine because maintaining privacy in medical treatments and diagnoses is a value of high order that would be effectively unreviewable after final judgment.

positions.label: Not immediately appealable
positions.summary: Holds that orders denying motions to seal are not immediately appealable because they do not satisfy the collateral order doctrine's requirement of being effectively unreviewable on appeal from final judgment.

splits.legalQuestion: What legal standards govern claims of discrimination or unfair treatment in the operation of hospitality or business establishments?
splits.description: The Supreme Court granted certiorari to resolve questions about legal standards for business establishment discrimination claims, indicating the Second Circuit's approach was sufficiently unsettled or in conflict with other circuits to warrant review. The decision could impact hospitality, retail, and other service industries nationwide.

positions.label: Second Circuit approach
positions.summary: The Second Circuit applied standards for discrimination or unfair treatment claims in hospitality that SCOTUS found warranted review, suggesting a potential conflict with other circuits.

positions.label: Alternative approach
positions.summary: Other circuits may apply different standards for evaluating discrimination claims in business establishments, creating the conflict that prompted SCOTUS review.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a state law categorically barring transgender women from women's sports teams violates the Equal Protection Clause as applied to transgender women who have medically mitigated sex-based biological advantages, and whether as-applied equal protection challenges are viable under intermediate scrutiny.
splits.description: Circuits are divided on whether categorical bans on transgender athlete participation survive intermediate scrutiny when applied to individuals who have undergone medical transition. The case also raises the broader question of whether sex-based classifications affecting transgender individuals warrant heightened scrutiny.

positions.label: Categorical ban violates Equal Protection as applied
positions.summary: Holds that a categorical ban fails intermediate scrutiny as applied to transgender women who have medically mitigated biological advantages, because the state has not shown the ban is substantially related to its interest in competitive fairness for this subclass.

positions.label: Categorical ban does not violate Equal Protection
positions.summary: Holds that biological sex-based classifications in athletics are substantially related to the important governmental interest in fair competition and the safety of female athletes, even as applied to transgender women.

circuits.name: Fourth Circuit
circuits.caseName: B.P.J. v. West Virginia State Board of Education

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLUIPA) clearly authorizes individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials, and whether Congress has the constitutional power under the Spending Clause to impose such personal liability.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether RLUIPA's text provides sufficiently clear notice to authorize damages claims against prison officials in their individual capacities, implicating Spending Clause limits on Congress's ability to impose personal liability on individuals who are not direct recipients of federal funds.

positions.label: RLUIPA authorizes individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA's text and structure provide clear authorization for damages suits against state prison officials in their individual capacities.

positions.label: RLUIPA does not authorize individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA does not clearly authorize individual-capacity damages suits against prison officials, and the Spending Clause limits Congress's ability to impose such liability on non-recipients of federal funds.

circuits.name: Fifth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Sossamon v. Lone Star State of Texas

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Landor v. Louisiana Department of Corrections and Public Safety

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may consider factors related to potential errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as part of the 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' analysis for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether compassionate release motions may be used to raise claims that overlap with habeas corpus challenges, such as alleged sentencing errors or constitutional violations in the underlying conviction. Some circuits permit consideration of such factors, while others hold that § 3582(c)(1)(A) cannot be used as a substitute for § 2255 habeas relief.

positions.label: May consider conviction/sentence errors
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may consider legal errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as one factor in the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis for compassionate release.

positions.label: Cannot use compassionate release for habeas-type claims
positions.summary: Holds that § 3582(c)(1)(A) is not an alternative avenue for claims properly raised under § 2255, and errors in conviction or sentencing cannot constitute extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Aviation Administration Authorization Act of 1994 (FAAAA) preempts state-law negligence claims against freight brokers who arrange transportation of property by motor carriers.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the FAAAA's broad preemption clause, which prohibits states from enacting laws 'related to a price, route, or service of any... broker,' preempts common-law negligence claims against freight brokers for injuries arising from the carrier's operations. This split affects the liability exposure of freight brokers nationwide.

positions.label: FAAAA preempts broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are preempted by the FAAAA because they relate to the broker's services in arranging transportation.

circuits.name: Ninth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Miller v. C.H. Robinson Worldwide, Inc.

positions.label: FAAAA does not preempt broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are not preempted by the FAAAA because they are generally applicable common-law duties rather than regulations targeting broker services.

circuits.name: Eleventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA) preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims based on allegedly inadequate product labeling when the EPA has not required the specific warning.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether FIFRA's preemption provision bars state-law failure-to-warn claims against pesticide manufacturers when the claim is based on the absence of a warning that the EPA did not require. The split affects product liability litigation involving agricultural chemicals and consumer pesticide products.

positions.label: FIFRA preempts failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims that would effectively require labeling different from or in addition to what FIFRA and EPA regulations permit.

positions.label: FIFRA does not preempt failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA does not preempt state-law failure-to-warn claims because such claims impose requirements 'parallel to' rather than 'in addition to' FIFRA's labeling requirements.

circuits.name: Third Circuit
circuits.caseName: DeKalb Genetics Corp. v. Bayer CropScience

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Monsanto Company v. John L. Durnell

splits.legalQuestion: Whether 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3), which prohibits unlawful users of controlled substances from possessing firearms, violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users.
splits.description: Following the Supreme Court's decision in Bruen, circuits have split on whether § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by users of controlled substances — particularly marijuana — is constitutional. Some circuits have upheld the law under historical tradition analysis, while others have found it unconstitutional as applied to marijuana users.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is constitutional
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by unlawful drug users is consistent with the nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation and survives Second Amendment scrutiny.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is unconstitutional as applied
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3) violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users because the government has not demonstrated a historical tradition of disarming persons who use intoxicating substances.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether workers who distribute baked goods to retail stores qualify as 'transportation workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce' under Section 1 of the Federal Arbitration Act, thereby exempting them from mandatory arbitration agreements.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the scope of the FAA's Section 1 transportation worker exemption, specifically whether workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of a broader interstate distribution chain are 'transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce.' The split affects the enforceability of arbitration agreements for a broad class of last-mile delivery workers.

positions.label: Broad interpretation — last-mile workers exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of an interstate distribution chain are transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce exempt from the FAA.

positions.label: Narrow interpretation — last-mile workers not exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who merely distribute goods locally to retail stores are not transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce and remain subject to FAA arbitration agreements.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 47(b) of the Investment Company Act creates a private right of action allowing parties to a contract that violates the ICA to sue in federal court for rescission of that contract.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether § 47(b) of the ICA provides an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts made in violation of the Act. This affects the ability of private parties to enforce the ICA's protections against abusive investment company practices through direct federal court actions.

positions.label: Section 47(b) creates a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) creates an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts that violate the Investment Company Act, allowing private parties to sue directly.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

positions.label: Section 47(b) does not create a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) is a voidability provision rather than a private right of action, and only the SEC can enforce the ICA's prohibitions.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, as construed under the Gingles framework, can constitutionally compel race-based redistricting as a remedy for vote dilution, and whether compliance with Section 2 constitutes a compelling governmental interest justifying the use of race in drawing district lines.
splits.description: This case raises the question of whether race-conscious redistricting mandated by Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act is constitutionally permissible under the Equal Protection Clause. Lower courts have applied the Gingles framework to require consideration of race, but the constitutionality of this framework as applied is increasingly contested.

positions.label: Section 2 compels constitutionally permissible race-conscious redistricting
positions.summary: Holds that compliance with Section 2 of the VRA, as interpreted under the Gingles framework, constitutes a compelling interest that justifies the use of race in drawing district lines.

positions.label: Section 2's compelled race-based redistricting raises constitutional concerns
positions.summary: Holds or suggests that the Gingles framework's requirement of race-based redistricting may exceed constitutional limits under the Equal Protection Clause, particularly after Dobbs-era equal protection jurisprudence.

circuits.name: Eighth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Arkansas State Conference of the NAACP v. Arkansas Board of Apportionment
